covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

parts.quote: Yes, they went to the estimates hearing.
Goodnight, and good luck.
Actually, that's an interesting point.
Excuse me, should I come with you?
Today I went to work.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: The page does not define ‘very short’. A checker needs a reviewed interpretation of that exception; no numerical threshold is supplied here.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory word, greeting or expression addressing someone is not followed by a comma, outside the very-short-sentence exception.
when: An introductory word, greeting or expression addressing someone precedes the rest of the sentence.
A comma after an introductory word is optional when the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the heading and body; G-3 keeps the very-short-sentence permission as an exception.

covers.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
Many introductory phrases can be moved to the end of sentences without changing the meaning. In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase.
Conditional clauses are adverbial clauses (for example, beginning with ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’). They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral. It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.

parts.quote: During the meeting, we discussed Item 9.
We discussed Item 9 during the meeting.
During the meeting, we discussed item 9.
Although they were shaking and sweating, the firefighters were relieved to feel the first drops of a downpour.
Unless the consultation starts early, it will not finish on time.

rules.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory adverbial phrase or clause is not separated from the following main clause by a comma.
when: An adverbial phrase or clause introduces the sentence.
This includes introductory conditional clauses.
A phrase ending in a numeral and immediately followed by another numeral needs the comma regardless of sentence length.
A phrase moved to the end of the sentence without changing the meaning does not need a preceding comma.
The separately stated ‘for example’ rule handles that specific phrase.
rules.why: G-2 combines introductory adverbial, conditional and adjacent-numeral cases; G-3 records the end-position exception.

covers.quote: Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

parts.quote: There were 16.5 million people enrolled to vote in Australian elections on 18 April 2019.

examples.note: The manual labels this ‘Not this’ for readability while explicitly acknowledging that it is grammatically correct.

parts.quote: On 18 April 2019, 16.5 million people were enrolled to vote in Australian elections.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.specification: The surrounding prose identifies the structure as an introductory phrase ending in a numeral immediately followed by another numeral at the start of the main clause.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with an introductory numerical or date phrase followed immediately by another numeral, creating a string of numbers and dates.
when: An introductory numerical or date phrase ends with a numeral and the main clause starts with another numeral.
The structure remains discouraged even when its comma is grammatically correct.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the heading and body; this readability finding is distinct from a missing introductory comma.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

parts.quote: The committee, said the secretary, was incompetent.

examples.note: This is a correct sentence with a different meaning, not a comma violation.

parts.quote: The committee said the secretary was incompetent.
The business report, which the manager had edited, explained the agency’s strategy.
Introduced pests, such as varroa mite, threaten Australian honey production.
The report that the manager had edited explained the agency’s strategy.
Introduced pests from South Asia threaten Australian honey production.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A non-essential clause lacks one or both delimiting commas, or an essential clause is incorrectly set off with commas.
when: A clause supplies supplementary information within a sentence.
A removable clause that leaves the sentence’s meaning unchanged is non-essential.
A clause essential to identifying the intended meaning must not be set off as non-essential.
rules.why: G-1 selects the specific child rather than its grouping parent; G-2 keeps essential and non-essential cases together.

covers.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

parts.quote: The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia, in June 2014.
The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia in June 2014.
My colleague, Mx Lesley May, will exercise my proxy vote.
My colleague will exercise my proxy vote.

rules.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
rules.violation_condition: A supplementary noun phrase defining the noun phrase immediately before it lacks one or both commas needed to enclose it.
when: Two adjacent noun phrases define the same thing and the second supplies non-essential information within the sentence.
Removing the second noun phrase leaves a grammatically correct sentence.
rules.why: G-1 keeps the specific noun-phrase check; G-4 absorbs its body restatement and removal test.

covers.quote: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

parts.quote: They’re not here, are they?
We’ll be reporting back, won’t we?

rules.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence-final question tag is not preceded by a comma.
when: A question is tagged onto the end of a statement within the same sentence.
rules.why: G-1 keeps question tags separate from the grouping parent; G-4 uses the body’s explicit punctuation instruction.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.

parts.quote: Some colours, for example, are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.
For example, some colours are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: Explanatory ‘for example’ lacks a required surrounding comma, or lacks its following comma when sentence-initial, outside the bullet-list-colon case.
when: ‘For example’ functions as an explanatory phrase in a sentence.
Within a sentence, it generally has a comma before and after it.
At the beginning of a sentence, only the following comma is needed.
When it introduces a bullet list, a colon replaces the following comma; the separate colon rule checks that boundary.
rules.why: G-2 combines sentence-internal and sentence-initial positions; the bullet-list colon is a distinct punctuation check.

parts.quote: Some colours are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish, for example:
red
green
orange
brown
blue
purple.

rules.quote: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list lead-in ending in ‘for example’ lacks a colon after that phrase.
when: ‘For example’ immediately introduces a bullet list.
rules.why: The required bullet-list colon is a separate finding from missing commas around a phrase; E-3 keeps its lead-in and items together.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms

parts.quote: Exports of rare earths (e.g. lithium, europium) have soared.
Exports of rare earths (e.g., lithium and europium) have soared.

rules.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: A comma immediately follows a Latin shortened form.
when: A Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ is used.
rules.why: G-4 selects the body because it specifies that the prohibited comma follows the shortened form.

covers.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

parts.quote: The Senate debated the Bill at length, but the party whips eventually called for a vote.
The company closed its Perth office and sacked the chief financial officer.
The company closed its Perth office, sacked the chief financial officer, and opened a branch in Singapore.

rules.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
rules.violation_condition: Coordinated principal clauses with different subjects lack a comma before their conjunction, or a series of more than two principal clauses sharing a subject lacks the required separating commas.
when: Principal clauses are joined by a coordinating conjunction such as ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’ or ‘so’.
Two clauses with different subjects need a comma before the conjunction.
Two clauses sharing a subject do not require a repeated subject or a comma.
More than two principal clauses sharing a subject require separating commas, including before the final conjunction.
rules.why: G-2 explicitly groups different-subject, shared-subject and more-than-two-clause cases; G-3 preserves the shared-subject permission.

rules.quote: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence formed by joining principal clauses with commas and coordinating conjunctions contains more than 25 words.
when: A sentence joins principal clauses using commas and coordinating conjunctions.
rules.why: This states a measurable property of the resulting sentence, not merely writer advice, and is distinct from comma placement.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

parts.quote: The report was finished last week, but the minister has not approved its release.
The report was finished last week, the minister has not approved its release.

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: A comma alone joins two stand-alone sentences without a coordinating conjunction.
when: The material on each side of a linking comma could stand as a sentence.
A coordinating conjunction permits the comma linkage.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the heading and explicit body instruction; the conjunction exception belongs to this single splice check.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.

parts.quote: The delegation visited Brisbane, Canberra and Adelaide.
The consultation involved businesses, sole traders and not-for-profits.
The applicant was willing to learn, eager to work and well prepared.

rules.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list.
rules.violation_condition: Successive items in a sentence list lack a separating comma at a boundary other than the final conjunction boundary.
when: Items form a sentence list, including a sentence list within a fragment in a bullet list.
The separate Oxford-comma rule handles the boundary before the final coordinated item.
This is not a requirement to put commas at the ends of bullet-list items.
rules.why: G-1 selects a child of the grouping heading; G-4 absorbs its heading, while the final-item comma is checked separately.

covers.quote: Restrict the use of the Oxford comma
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item.
For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

parts.quote: The industries most affected are retail trade, wholesale trade, and accommodation and food services.

examples.note: The manual gives the meaning that all crops are for stockfeed.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat and hay for stockfeed.

examples.note: The manual gives the meaning that only the hay is for stockfeed.

parts.quote: The analysis outlined demand for barley, wheat, and hay for stockfeed.

rules.quote: Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.
rules.specification: The normal omission has stated exceptions for an internal ‘and’ in the final item and for a defining phrase applying only to that item. The discussion also identifies prevention of ambiguity in complex lists as the purpose of the Oxford comma.
rules.violation_condition: A comma precedes the final coordinated list item without a disambiguating reason, or the comma is missing where the final item contains an internal ‘and’ or has a defining phrase intended to apply only to it.
when: A sentence list has a final item introduced by a conjunction.

Include it when a defining phrase applies only to the final item.

rules.quote: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

anchor.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates

anchor.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

examples.note: This is a correct sentence with a different meaning, not a comma violation.

tags.violation_condition: A non-essential clause lacks one or both delimiting commas, or an essential clause is incorrectly set off with commas.

when: A clause supplies supplementary information within a sentence.

A clause essential to identifying the intended meaning must not be set off as non-essential.
rules.why: G-1 selects the specific child rather than its grouping parent; G-2 keeps essential and non-essential cases together.

anchor.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow

anchor.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.

tags.violation_condition: Explanatory ‘for example’ lacks a required surrounding comma, or lacks its following comma when sentence-initial, outside the bullet-list-colon case.

Within a sentence, it generally has a comma before and after it.
At the beginning of a sentence, only the following comma is needed.

If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.
